newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Relieved Russian doctors say surgery went well.
newsitem.headline: Relieved Russian doctors say surgery went well.

text.p: Top surgeons, clearly relieved at the course of President Boris Yeltsin's long-awaited heart operation, said on Tuesday that everything had gone well.
But Russian cardiologist Renat Akchurin, the man with the awesome task of slicing open the president and repairing damaged arteries, admitted the responsibility had been hard to bear.
"I was trying to forget that it was the president of Russia and think this is an ordinary patient," Akchurin, grey with fatigue after a seven-hour operation, told a news conference.
Yeltsin, 65, announced exactly two months ago that he needed an operation to improve the blood supply to his heart and allow him to live a normal life.

But the experts, facing a raft of possible complications from anaemia to thyroid problems, waited until they were sure his body was ready to withstand the strain before going ahead with the multiple bypass operation.
It will take several days for the final outcome of the surgery to become clear. "We usually speak about a forecast on the fifth or sixth day after the operation," Akchurin said.
But the mood among the doctors at Moscow's Cardiology Research Centre was clearly upbeat.
"The operation went better than I expected," said cardiology centre head Yevgeny Chazov, 67, who kept increasingly senile Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev alive for a decade in the 1970s.
Akchurin, 50, had led a team of a dozen Russian doctors conducting the bypass operation. He said Yeltsin's heart had been stopped for 68 minutes while the surgeons worked.
Observers included veteran U.S. cardiologist Michael DeBakey, who conducted the world's first successful bypass operation in 1964.
"I find it a great pleasure to confirm that the operation was a complete success," DeBakey, who is 23 years older than his patient, told the news conference.
"President Yeltsin will be able to return to his office and carry out his duties in normal fashion."
DeBakey said Yeltsin was receiving "absolutely expert care" at the hospital, on the western outskirts of Moscow.
Akchurin said his team had made more than the expected three or four bypasses but declined to give a figure, saying it was up to Yeltsin to decide whether to make it public.

Doctors have said the post-operative stage is the one of most crucial parts of Yeltsin's treatment and specialists advising the Russian doctors on the operation include two German surgeons who have done a lot of work in this sphere.

Akchurin said Yeltsin would decide himself when to resume his presidential responsibilities, which he transferred to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin minutes before the operation started on Tuesday.
"He will decide himself, in all probability it will be tomorrow or the day after -- touch wood," he said.
